entry.title: More compute, better AI: how much better?

link.title: More compute, better AI: how much better?

entry.content:
“Scaling laws” are the reason AI companies are building gigawatt data centers. The idea is that a language model improves predictably as it gets more computing power, more parameters and more data. But how much better? If we had ten or a hundred times more computing power than today, what would we get? This post works through the answer using the original papers and the latest data, as of October 2026.

The scaling law in one sentence

In 2020, Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI showed that a language model’s loss, a measure of how badly it predicts the next word, falls as a power law of training compute, over eight orders of magnitude (Kaplan et al. 2020). In 2022, DeepMind’s “Chinchilla” study refined the recipe: for a given compute budget, parameters and training data should grow together, roughly 20 tokens of text per parameter (Hoffmann et al. 2022). A later replication by Epoch AI corrected the fitted constants but confirmed the 20-to-1 rule (Besiroglu et al. 2024).

The corrected fit makes the returns concrete. Loss has an irreducible floor, set by the inherent unpredictability of text, and only the gap above that floor can be closed. Each 10× increase in compute closes about a third of the remaining gap; 100× closes about half (Figure 1a, my calculation from the fit). In other words, every halving of what is left to gain costs about a hundredfold more compute.

Figure 1. (a) Pretraining loss predicted by the Chinchilla scaling law (with Epoch AI’s corrected constants) when compute is allocated optimally between model size and data, with the approximate training compute of some well-known models and of the largest run Epoch AI judges feasible by 2030. (b) The number of training tokens the same law calls for, compared with the estimated stock of public human-written text. The fit describes one family of models; it shows the shape of the curve, not the exact loss of any frontier model. Figure by Daeha Kim, calculated from Besiroglu et al. (2024), with compute estimates from Brown et al. (2020) and Epoch AI, and the data stock from Villalobos et al. (2024).

Does lower loss mean a smarter model?

Loss falls smoothly, but people experience abilities, and abilities sometimes seem to appear suddenly with scale. A 2023 study showed that most of these apparent jumps are artifacts of all-or-nothing scoring: more than 92% of the claimed “emergent abilities” came from just two metrics that give credit only for a perfectly right answer (Schaeffer et al. 2023). Measured with continuous scores, the same abilities improve gradually.

Real-world capability has nonetheless improved fast. METR measures the length of software tasks, in human working time, that AI agents can complete half the time. That “time horizon” doubled about every seven months between 2019 and 2025 (Kwa et al. 2025), and on METR’s updated task suite the doubling time shortened to about 130 days since 2023 and 89 days since 2024 (METR 2026). By mid-2026 the best models were near the ceiling of what the suite can measure. METR stopped updating its measurements in September, so there is no reliable figure for the months since.

Faster chips are only part of the story

The obvious way to get more compute is better hardware, but chips alone improve slowly. Epoch AI decomposed the growth of frontier training compute, about 4.2× per year since 2018 (Epoch AI 2025; Figure 2):

  • more chips per training run: 1.7× per year;
  • longer training runs: 1.5× per year;
  • faster chips: 1.4× per year.

In log terms, faster chips supply only about a quarter of the growth. At 1.4× per year, a tenfold improvement from chips alone takes about seven years. The frontier gets ten times more compute about every year and a half mainly by spending more: the cost of the largest training runs has grown about 2.4× per year (Cottier et al. 2024), and the largest single data centers now draw about a gigawatt.

Better algorithms add a further multiplier. The compute needed to reach a given level of language-model performance has halved about every eight months, equivalent to about 2.8× more “effective” compute every year (Ho et al. 2024). Combining both, effective compute has grown roughly tenfold or more per year, my calculation.

Figure 2. Median yearly growth of training compute for frontier models since 2018 and its three components, and the yearly gain from better algorithms expressed as equivalent compute. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported by Epoch AI (2025) and Ho et al. (2024).

A second axis: thinking longer

Since 2024, a second kind of scaling has mattered as much as the first. Reasoning models such as OpenAI’s o1 improve when they are allowed to spend more compute on each question. On the AIME 2024 math competition, o1 solved 74% of problems with one attempt, 83% with a majority vote over 64 attempts, and 93% when a learned scorer picked the best of 1,000 (OpenAI 2024). On the ARC-AGI puzzle benchmark, o3 rose from 75.7% to 87.5% when given about 172 times more compute per task (ARC Prize 2024).

The pattern is the same as in pretraining: gains are roughly linear in the logarithm of compute, so each additional step costs ten to a hundred times more (Figure 3). Reinforcement learning, the training method behind these reasoning models, shows a similar shape but levels off at a ceiling set by the training recipe (Khatri et al. 2025).

Figure 3. Accuracy of OpenAI’s o1 on AIME 2024 and of o3 (preview) on ARC-AGI-1 as more samples are used per problem. The o1 points use different ways of combining samples (a single attempt, a majority vote and re-ranking by a learned scorer). Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported by OpenAI (2024) and ARC Prize (2024).

The limits ahead: power, data and money

Epoch AI estimates that a training run of about 2×10²⁹ FLOP, roughly 400 times the largest known run of 2025, is likely feasible by 2030, but power is the first constraint to bind: such a run would need about 6 gigawatts, while today’s largest single sites draw about one (Sevilla et al. 2024).

Data may bind even earlier. The stock of public human-written text is estimated at about 300 trillion tokens (Villalobos et al. 2024). A compute-optimal run of 10²⁸ FLOP would already need about 150 trillion tokens, half of it (Figure 1b). Repeating data helps for a while, since up to about four passes over the same text is nearly as good as new data (Muennighoff et al. 2023), and synthetic data and reinforcement learning on checkable tasks are partly a response to this limit.

Have the returns diminished?

In late 2024 and 2025, reports suggested that simply making pretraining bigger was paying off less than expected, and OpenAI’s GPT-4.5 was widely seen as a modest step. In November 2025, Ilya Sutskever described the period from 2020 to 2025 as an “age of scaling” now giving way to an “age of research.” Yet over the same period, measured capability accelerated: an Epoch AI analysis found that several capability indices, including METR’s time horizon, sped up around 2024, driven largely by reasoning models and concentrated in code and mathematics (Epoch AI 2026).

Both observations fit the scaling law. Returns to pretraining compute were always diminishing in the sense shown in Figure 1, so a few times more compute buys a modest step. What changed is that labs found a second, cheaper axis, reinforcement learning and inference-time compute, and better algorithms on top.

So how much does more hardware buy?

  • On paper: each 10× in training compute closes about a third of the remaining gap in loss. Large, steady gains require exponential increases in compute.
  • In practice: that 10× arrives about every 18 months, but mostly from more chips and more money; faster chips alone would take about seven years to deliver it.
  • Beyond pretraining: letting models think longer adds similar log-linear gains per question, at a cost paid every time the model is used.
  • Limits: power and data, not chip speed, are the constraints most likely to bind before 2030.

Scaling laws do not promise that more hardware makes AI arbitrarily capable. They promise steady improvement for exponentially rising cost, and so far that bargain, combined with better algorithms, has been good enough to keep progress fast.

Questions to think about

  1. If each halving of the remaining loss costs a hundredfold more compute, what would make it worth paying?
  2. Inference-time compute is paid every time a model is used. How does that change the economics compared with training compute, which is paid once?
  3. Many scientific models also improve with resolution and data following power laws. Where in your own field have you seen diminishing returns of this kind?

entry.title: Model distillation: how AI models learn from each other, and what they lose

link.title: Model distillation: how AI models learn from each other, and what they lose

entry.content:
In July 2026, the White House science adviser accused the Chinese company Moonshot AI of building its Kimi K3 model by “distilling” Anthropic’s Claude Fable. China’s embassy in Washington called the allegation “entirely unfounded” (Business Today 2026), and several AI researchers doubted it, noting that K3 appeared only about two weeks after Fable became public and that distillation alone is unlikely to produce such a strong model so quickly (AI Weekly 2026). True or not, the episode shows how central one technique has become to the competition between AI labs. This post explains what distillation is, why it works, whether it can be stopped, and what models built this way tend to lack.

What distillation is

Distillation means training a smaller or newer model, the “student,” to imitate a stronger one, the “teacher.” The idea was popularized by Hinton and colleagues in 2015 (Hinton et al. 2015). Their key observation was that a teacher’s full output carries more information than its final answer. When a language model completes “The capital of Australia is …,” it assigns a high probability to Canberra, but also a noticeable probability to Sydney and almost none to Perth (Figure 1a). Those small numbers encode how the teacher sees the world, which mistakes are plausible and which are not. Hinton called it “dark knowledge.” A student trained to match the whole distribution learns faster and from fewer examples than one trained only on correct answers.

Inside a lab, distillation is routine and legitimate. The fast, cheap versions of frontier models are typically distilled from larger ones, and DeepSeek released a family of small open models distilled from its R1 reasoning model (DeepSeek-AI 2025).

The controversial version works from the outside. A competitor cannot see another lab’s probabilities, but it can send millions of questions through the public interface, collect the answers, and train its own model on them. The student then sees much less than in the classic setup: one sampled answer instead of a full distribution, and often no reasoning at all (Figure 1b).

Figure 1. (a) An illustrative next-word distribution from a teacher model: besides the right answer, it shows which wrong answers are close. (b) What a student model can learn from, from a lab distilling its own model to a competitor working through a chat interface. The probabilities and bar lengths are illustrative. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic based on Hinton et al. (2015).

Why it has become a dispute

The attraction is obvious: answers from a frontier model are far cheaper to collect than the compute, data and expertise needed to develop the same abilities independently. In February 2026, Anthropic reported that three Chinese labs, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and MiniMax, had generated more than 16 million exchanges with Claude through about 24,000 fraudulent accounts, targeting its strongest abilities: agentic reasoning, tool use and coding (Anthropic 2026; Figure 2). These are Anthropic’s attributions; the labs have not confirmed them. The July accusation about Kimi K3 went further, but its evidence has not been made public.

Figure 2. Exchanges with Claude that Anthropic attributed to distillation campaigns by three AI labs, as reported in February 2026. According to Anthropic, the campaigns targeted agentic coding and tool use (MiniMax); agentic reasoning, tool use, coding, computer use and vision (Moonshot AI); and reasoning and the grading of answers for reinforcement learning (DeepSeek). Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Anthropic (2026).

The dispute has an uncomfortable side for the accusers, too. Frontier models were themselves trained on vast amounts of text written by others, and the line between learning from public outputs and copying is contested. What makes the current cases different, in the labs’ view, is the use of fake accounts and the violation of terms of service to extract a competitor’s specific capabilities at scale.

Can it be prevented?

Not completely. Anything a model shows its users, it also shows a potential student. What labs can do is make distillation slower, costlier and less useful:

  • Detection. Classifiers that recognize distillation patterns, such as huge numbers of similar prompts or systematic attempts to extract reasoning, and that link many accounts to one operator (Anthropic 2026).
  • Access control. Stronger identity checks for the account types most often abused, and sharing of indicators between labs and cloud providers.
  • Hiding the reasoning. Since 2024, several labs show only a summary of their models’ step-by-step reasoning. OpenAI cited competitive advantage, alongside safety monitoring, when it decided not to show the raw reasoning of its o1 models (OpenAI 2024).
  • Poisoned outputs. Researchers have proposed “antidistillation sampling,” which subtly changes how a model picks its words so that the answers remain useful to people but are much less useful as training data for a student (Savani et al. 2025).

Each defense has a cost for legitimate users, who also want to see the reasoning and use the model at scale. The realistic goal is to keep distillation from being a shortcut, not to make it impossible.

What distilled models lack

Distillation lets a model catch up quickly. But copying has limits.

Style transfers more easily than substance. In a careful 2023 study, researchers fine-tuned open models on ChatGPT outputs. Human raters judged the imitations close to ChatGPT, because they had learned its confident, well-structured style, yet on targeted tests of factual knowledge, coding and problem solving they improved little or not at all (Gudibande et al. 2024). The authors concluded that closing the gap requires a stronger base model, not more imitation. A distilled model can therefore look better than it is, which also makes some benchmark scores and first impressions misleading.

The student learns only what it is asked. A campaign aimed at coding and agents transfers coding and agents. Rare facts, niche fields, other languages and unusual situations are covered thinly, and the student sees only sampled answers without the teacher’s uncertainty. As discussed in an earlier post on hallucination, rare facts are exactly where models make things up.

It inherits mistakes, and copies of copies degrade. A student copies its teacher’s errors and biases along with its strengths. When models are trained repeatedly on the output of other models, the rare parts of the original data, the tails of the distribution, gradually disappear, a process known as model collapse (Shumailov et al. 2024).

It stays one step behind. A student rarely surpasses its teacher in what it copies, and it can only copy what already exists. Distillation is a way to follow the frontier, not to move it.

Safety behavior may not come along. Anthropic argues that illicitly distilled models are unlikely to keep the safeguards built into the original, such as refusals to help with weapons or cyberattacks (Anthropic 2026).

Provenance becomes a risk. For companies, universities and public agencies, a model built in violation of another provider’s terms carries legal and reputational risk, and possibly sanctions. That matters when choosing a model for sensitive work.

Bottom line

Distillation is an old and useful idea: a small model learns faster from a teacher’s full judgments than from right answers alone. Done from the outside, through millions of questions, it lets new models catch up with the frontier at a fraction of the cost, which is why it has become a source of accusations between labs and governments. It cannot be fully prevented, only made harder. And it has clear limits: distilled models copy style more easily than substance, cover what they were asked and little else, inherit their teachers’ errors and stay one step behind. For users, the lesson is to test such models on their own tasks, especially rare and specialized ones, before trusting their benchmark scores.

Questions to think about

  1. If a model’s benchmark scores come partly from imitating a stronger model, how would you design a test that reveals the difference?
  2. Where should the line be drawn between learning from public outputs, which all models do, and illicit distillation?
  3. Would you use a model of uncertain provenance for research with sensitive data? What would you need to know first?

entry.title: How the brain invented learning, part II: reinforcing in A Brief History of Intelligence

link.title: How the brain invented learning, part II: reinforcing in A Brief History of Intelligence

entry.content:
In part I, we followed the first of the five breakthroughs in Max Bennett’s A Brief History of Intelligence (2023): steering. Bilaterian worms learned to move toward the good and away from the bad, and to store experience in the strength of their synapses. Their dopamine meant only “something good is nearby.”

This post covers the second breakthrough, reinforcing: how early vertebrates acquired trial-and-error learning, how AI researchers ran into the same problem, and how the same molecule, dopamine, was turned into a learning signal. As before, the summary is my own paraphrase of the book’s argument.

1. Breakthrough 2, Reinforcing: try it, then learn from the result

The stage for the second breakthrough is the early vertebrates that emerged about 500 million years ago, after the Cambrian explosion. The brains of these fish-like ancestors already had the basic blueprint that persists all the way to the human brain: a precursor of the cortex (the pallium), the basal ganglia, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, and hindbrain.

What this blueprint made possible was trial-and-error learning. The nematode’s associative learning was about learning that “good things follow this stimulus.” Vertebrates learn that “good things follow when I do this.” They learn the consequences not of stimuli but of their own actions.

From Thorndike to Minsky

In 1898, Edward Thorndike placed cats in puzzle boxes and watched. At first they poked at everything until they happened to release the latch, but with repetition their escape times fell. Actions followed by satisfying outcomes are repeated; actions followed by unpleasant ones fade. This is the law of effect, and fish learn the same way.

The trouble surfaced when people tried to put this principle into machines. In the early 1950s Marvin Minsky built SNARC, a neural-network machine that learned by reinforcement, and he later named the critical obstacle: the temporal credit assignment problem. When you win a game of chess, which of the dozens of earlier moves contributed to the win? The later the reward arrives, the harder it is to know which action to reinforce.

Sutton’s answer: learn from changes in prediction, not from the reward itself

Temporal difference (TD) learning, formalized by Richard Sutton in the 1980s, sidesteps the problem elegantly. Instead of waiting for the final reward, the learner keeps a running prediction of how good things are going to be, and learns from the difference between successive predictions. If the position suddenly looks better, the action just taken was probably a good one.

\[\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\]

Here \(V(s)\) is the predicted value of state \(s\), \(r\) is the immediate reward, and \(\gamma\) is the discount factor. \(\delta\), the TD error, measures how much better things turned out than expected. The architecture is often split in two: a critic that evaluates states, and an actor that adjusts its policy using the critic’s error.

In 1992, Gerald Tesauro at IBM used this method to build TD-Gammon, a neural network that plays backgammon. Learning by playing against itself, it reached a level close to the best human players. It was the first striking evidence that reinforcement learning really works.

2. Dopamine is the TD error

The most dramatic moment in the book is the discovery that an algorithm AI researchers had devised on paper was already running inside the brain.

In the 1980s and 1990s, Wolfram Schultz recorded the activity of dopamine neurons in the monkey midbrain. The setup was simple: a light (the cue) comes on, and a few seconds later juice (the reward) arrives. But the dopamine neurons’ behavior could not be explained as a response to reward.

  • Before learning: when juice arrives unexpectedly, dopamine neurons fire strongly.
  • After learning: they fire when the light comes on, and do not respond when the juice itself arrives.
  • When the light is not followed by juice: firing drops below baseline at the moment the juice should have come.

In all three cases, dopamine tracks not the reward received but the difference between the reward received and the reward expected.

These three patterns are exactly how the TD error \(\delta\) behaves. An unexpected reward is a positive error, a predicted reward is zero error, and the absence of an expected reward is a negative error. And the moment a prediction of “something good is coming” first appears, when the light comes on, is precisely when the outlook improves. When Schultz, Peter Dayan, and Read Montague published this correspondence in Science in 1997, the view took hold that dopamine is not a “pleasure chemical” but a reward prediction error signal.

Dopamine changed its meaning

Seen through Bennett’s evolutionary lens, the finding becomes even more interesting. In the nematode, dopamine was a state signal: “something good is nearby.” In vertebrates, the same molecule is repurposed as a learning signal: “things just got better than expected.” Evolution did not invent a new molecule. It changed the meaning of an existing broadcast channel.

The structure that receives this signal and adjusts behavior is the basal ganglia. The basal ganglia select one action from the available options and reinforce choices followed by a positive dopamine signal, so that those choices become easier to repeat. In reinforcement-learning terms, the basal ganglia play the actor, and the dopamine signal is the critic’s error.

Curiosity: surviving in a world of sparse rewards

Bennett argues that vertebrates also became curious at this stage. Fish explore novel things, and dopamine neurons respond not only to reward but also to novel stimuli. Novelty itself works as a kind of reward.

AI ran into the same problem. In environments where reward is very rare, such as the Atari game Montezuma’s Revenge, random exploration never reaches the first reward, so learning never gets started. Researchers’ fix was intrinsic motivation: a bonus for visiting states not seen before, in effect artificial curiosity. It is the same answer evolution reached 500 million years earlier.

3. The correspondence at a glance

The table below pairs each biological mechanism with its AI counterpart. The last column is my own judgment of how close the match is.

Biological mechanism AI counterpart How close
Law of effect (trial and error) Policy reinforcement Direct
Dopamine as reward prediction error TD error δ Quantitative match (Schultz et al., 1997)
Action selection in the basal ganglia Actor (actor-critic) Rough match; details debated
Dopamine response to novelty Intrinsic motivation, exploration bonus Functional match

4. Closing: similar, but not the same

Following the two breakthroughs reveals a single thread. Neurons arose for fast response, the bilaterian brain for steering by good and bad, synaptic plasticity for storing experience, and dopamine’s reinterpretation for learning from delayed reward. Each step reuses the parts of the one before rather than discarding them.

Still, it is too early to say that “the brain is a reinforcement learning algorithm.” A few differences are clear.

  • Learning rule: synapses change using only local information. Whether the brain has anything like backpropagation, which sends the output error precisely back through the layers, remains an open question.
  • Data efficiency: TD-Gammon needed hundreds of thousands of self-play games. A fish learns in a handful of trials.
  • Forgetting: animals keep old memories in suppressed form while learning new ones. Artificial networks are still weak here.
  • Dopamine’s other faces: dopamine does more than signal reward prediction error. It is involved in movement, motivation, and novelty, and how to interpret the signal is still an active research question.

Even so, the correspondence is illuminating. AI researchers did not reach these answers by copying the brain; they reached them by trying to solve the same problems. That evolution and engineering converged independently on the same solutions suggests that those solutions may come from the structure of the problems themselves.

Bennett’s next breakthrough, simulating, concerns the mammalian neocortex and its ability to simulate the future in the mind: trying things out in imagination rather than in reality. That is the story of model-based reinforcement learning, and I plan to take it up in the next post.

Questions to think about

  1. Dopamine changed from a state signal in worms to a learning signal in vertebrates. What other cases do you know where evolution, or engineering, repurposed an existing channel for a new job?
  2. A fish learns in a handful of trials, while TD-Gammon needed hundreds of thousands of games. What might explain the difference?
  3. TD learning learns from changes in prediction rather than from the final outcome. Where in your own field could a model learn from forecast updates rather than from observed outcomes alone?

Schultz 등(1997)은 원숭이의 도파민 뉴런이 보상 자체가 아니라 “예상보다 얼마나 좋았는가”에 반응한다는 것을 보였고, 이는 Sutton이 고안한 시간차(TD) 학습의 오차 신호와 같다. 진화는 새로운 물질을 만들지 않고, 선충 때부터 있던 도파민 신호의 뜻을 “근처에 좋은 것이 있다”에서 “예상보다 좋았다”로 바꾸었다. 뇌와 강화학습 사이에는 차이도 많지만, 둘이 서로 모른 채 같은 해법에 이르렀다는 것은 그 해법이 문제 자체의 성격에서 나온다는 것을 시사한다.

entry.title: Heat-stressed workers add about $41 to the social cost of carbon

link.title: Heat-stressed workers add about $41 to the social cost of carbon

entry.content:
How much damage does one more ton of CO₂ do? Economists answer with the social cost of carbon: the present value of all future harm caused by emitting one extra ton today. It is the number behind carbon prices, cost–benefit analyses of regulations and some infrastructure decisions, so what goes into it matters.

Until now, one obvious harm was missing. When it is hot and humid, people work more slowly and take more breaks, and outdoor workers in particular lose hours. A study in Nature Climate Change led by Frances Moore puts a price on this lost productivity for the first time within a modern framework for the social cost of carbon, and at the same time revises the estimate for agriculture (Moore et al. 2026). The two changes nearly cancel, but they change what the number is made of.

Heat stress is about humidity, not only temperature

The authors measure heat stress with the wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT), the standard metric for workplace safety. WBGT combines air temperature and sunlight, which heat the body, with humidity and wind, which control how well sweat can cool it. A hot, dry day can be safer for a worker than a slightly cooler, humid one.

They computed WBGT every three hours on a 0.25° grid from 15 bias-corrected climate models, then translated it into lost productivity using two response functions that act as upper and lower bounds. One is based on the international standard (ISO) for how much rest workers need at a given WBGT and work intensity. The other, used by the Lancet Countdown, is based on field observations of rice harvesters in India and miners in South Africa. Productivity loss was calculated separately for indoor and outdoor work at three levels of effort, with indoor exposure adjusted for how common air conditioning is in each country (from 0% in South Sudan to 90% in Japan).

Although WBGT rises most at high latitudes, the losses concentrate where it is already close to physiological limits: South and Southeast Asia, West Africa and the Amazon. Construction, with its heavy outdoor work, is hit hardest. These productivity losses were then fed into a global economic model, which lets production, trade and consumption adjust, before entering the calculation of the social cost of carbon.

The results

Labour costs about US\$41 per ton of CO₂. For a ton emitted in 2025 (in 2020 dollars, with a 2% discount rate), the mean labour damage is US\$41, with a median of US\$32 and a 90% range from US\$1 to US\$108 (Figure 2a). The ISO function alone gives US\$52, the Lancet function US\$30. An independent working paper using a completely different method, based on observed weekly working hours, arrived at a similar US\$39. Labour is now the second-largest component of the social cost of carbon, after heat-related deaths (US\$98) and ahead of the other sectors.

The burden falls on hot, humid, populous countries. India alone accounts for about US\$9 of the US\$41, followed by Nigeria (US\$6), China (US\$4) and Pakistan (US\$3) (Figure 2b). Per person, the damages are largest in Gulf states such as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates and in sub-Saharan Africa. With the ISO function, at 3°C of warming above 1995–2015, South Asia loses more than 6% of its income through heat-related labour losses alone, while Europe’s losses are negligible.

Agriculture costs less than thought. The previous estimate of agricultural damages relied on about 1,000 crop-yield projections from 56 studies compiled for the IPCC’s Fifth Assessment Report. The update uses 8,703 projections from 202 studies compiled for the Sixth. With this much larger evidence base, projected yield losses at high warming are smaller and much less uncertain. Agricultural damages fall from US\$95 to US\$29 per ton, and the 95th percentile drops by US\$260.

The total barely moves, but becomes more certain. Adding labour and revising agriculture lowers the mean social cost of carbon from US\$204 to US\$179 per ton (Figure 1). The long upper tail shrinks, and the probability that the true value is zero or negative falls from 0.6% to below 0.008%.

Figure 1. Mean social cost of carbon for a ton of CO₂ emitted in 2025 (2020 US dollars, 2% near-term discount rate), by damage sector, in the previous version of the GIVE model and in the revised version. Energy and sea-level rise are unchanged and shown as the remainder. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Moore et al. (2026).

Figure 2. (a) Labour component of the 2025 social cost of carbon: the preferred estimate (mean, median and 90% range), the estimates using each response function alone, and an independent estimate by Rode et al. using a different method. (b) The four countries with the largest contributions. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Moore et al. (2026).

What the numbers do and do not include

The authors are explicit about what could push the estimate up or down.

  • Cold benefits are not counted. Warmer winters might help some outdoor workers, but evidence suggests this effect is small.
  • Adaptation is partly included. The economic model shifts work to cooler hours of the day, moves production between sectors and regions, and substitutes machines for labour. It does not include the future spread of air conditioning, or changes such as shading construction sites, which would lower the cost, though not for free.
  • Health costs are only partly covered. Heat deaths are counted elsewhere in the social cost of carbon, but heat-related illness and injury are not.
  • Agriculture covers only four crops. Wheat, rice, maize and soybeans account for about half of cropped area; other crops, meat and dairy are not directly modeled.

Why this matters

The paper’s own conclusion is that a social cost of carbon near US\$200 per ton, the value adopted by the US Environmental Protection Agency in 2023, is well supported, and that a value of zero can be ruled out with high confidence. That is a pointed statement at a time when US federal guidance no longer monetizes climate damages in regulatory analysis.

There is also a quieter lesson about how such numbers improve. The agricultural estimate fell not because the climate risk disappeared but because the evidence base grew roughly eightfold and narrowed the uncertainty. The labour estimate rose because a real, well-documented harm was finally counted. Both changes come from better science, and they pull in opposite directions.

What a hydrologist takes from it

Humidity is a hydrological variable. Because WBGT depends on humidity, land and water management can change heat stress directly. Irrigation, for example, cools the surface but adds moisture to the air, and in India it has been shown to intensify humid heat extremes (Mishra et al. 2020). Decisions about irrigation therefore have consequences for the people who work in irrigated fields.

Wind matters for workers, too. In the previous post, wind sped up evaporation from ecosystems. In WBGT, wind does the same for the human body: it helps sweat evaporate. Calm, humid days are the most dangerous.

The losses follow the seasons. Even in the hottest regions, the thresholds that trigger productivity losses are crossed only during part of the year, and in agriculture those weeks often coincide with planting and harvest. Seasonal forecasts of humid heat could help farmers and builders plan around them.

Bottom line

Heat stress already slows workers, and climate change will make it worse, especially in hot, humid and populous regions of South Asia and Africa. Moore and colleagues estimate this cost at about US\$41 per ton of CO₂, making labour one of the largest components of the social cost of carbon. A better-supported agricultural estimate falls from US\$95 to US\$29, so the total settles near US\$180 per ton with much less uncertainty. Both revisions show that the social cost of carbon is not a fixed number but a running summary of what we know.

Questions to think about

  1. Two response functions, one physiological and one observational, give US\$52 and US\$30. Which would you trust more for Korean construction workers in July, and why?
  2. If expanding irrigation raises humid heat stress for farm workers, how would you weigh that against the yield benefits?
  3. Should a country’s own social cost of carbon count damages to workers in other countries? How would that change the number?

References

Moore, F. C., Haqiqi, I., Kong, Q., Rennels, L., Baldos, U., Ganapathi, H., Huber, M., & Hertel, T. (2026). New labour and agricultural damages improve climate cost estimates. Nature Climate Change, 16, 1170–1177. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-026-02749-z

Mishra, V., Ambika, A. K., Asoka, A., Aadhar, S., Buzan, J., Kumar, R., & Huber, M. (2020). Moist heat stress extremes in India enhanced by irrigation. Nature Geoscience, 13, 722–728. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-020-00650-8

Both figures are original. The Python scripts that produce them are available on GitHub: Figure 1, Figure 2.

entry.title: Wind makes ecosystems spend more water for the same carbon

link.title: Wind makes ecosystems spend more water for the same carbon

entry.content:
Ecosystems trade water for carbon. To take up CO₂ through their stomata, leaves have to let water vapor out, and the ratio between the two, the carbon gained per kilogram of water evaporated, is called water use efficiency (WUE). It is one of the most useful single numbers in ecohydrology. Rising WUE has usually been credited to rising CO₂, which lets plants narrow their stomata (Keenan et al. 2013), and to changes in temperature, sunlight and air dryness.

Wind has been mostly left out of that story. A new study in Nature Climate Change by Xiang Wang, Zheng Fu and colleagues brings it back (Wang et al. 2026). Using flux towers around the world and climate models, they show that on windier days, ecosystems use water less efficiently, and that the slow decline of winds over land in recent decades has been nudging WUE upward.

What they found

The authors used daily measurements of photosynthesis (gross primary productivity, GPP) and evapotranspiration (ET) from 146 eddy-covariance towers in the FLUXNET2015, AmeriFlux, ICOS and OzFlux networks. For each site they asked how WUE (GPP divided by ET) varied with wind speed during the growing season, after removing the effects of temperature, precipitation, sunlight, CO₂ and vapor-pressure deficit (VPD).

The answer was remarkably consistent. WUE fell significantly with wind at 79.5% of sites and rose significantly at only 5.5% (Figure 1a). The pattern held for almost every vegetation type and for different definitions of the growing season. Among all the drivers they examined, wind speed had the largest median standardized effect on WUE, ahead of sunlight, VPD and temperature.

On average, each additional meter per second of wind lowered WUE by about 0.26 grams of carbon per kilogram of water. The effect was strongest in evergreen needleleaf forests and in humid climates, and close to zero in arid climates (Figure 1b).

Figure 1. (a) Partial correlation between daily WUE and wind speed at 146 eddy-covariance sites during the growing season, after controlling for temperature, precipitation, CO₂, solar radiation and VPD. (b) Change in WUE per 1 m/s increase in wind speed (median and interquartile range) for all sites, two vegetation types and two climate classes. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Wang et al. (2026).

Why: wind mostly speeds up evaporation

WUE can fall because carbon uptake drops or because water loss rises. Splitting the two, the authors found that wind acts mainly on the water side: its effect on ET was almost three times as large as its effect on GPP (standardized sensitivities of +0.11 and −0.04).

The mechanism is familiar to anyone who has used the Penman–Monteith equation. Wind thins the layer of still air around leaves and increases the aerodynamic conductance, the ease with which water vapor is carried away from the canopy. In the paper, wind changed aerodynamic conductance strongly (standardized sensitivity 0.66) but barely changed canopy conductance, which reflects how far the stomata are open (0.03). In other words, the plants did not open up; the air simply carried more water away. Windier days were also drier: wind and VPD were positively correlated at 67% of sites, and higher VPD lowered WUE at 70% of them. Wind also coupled the canopy more tightly to the atmosphere, so that transpiration responded more to air dryness and less to sunlight. GPP declined a little as well, probably because drier air makes leaves partly close their stomata and because strong winds stress plants mechanically.

Why conifer forests and humid places respond most

The strong effect in needleleaf forests has a neat physical explanation, which the authors mention and which a simple calculation makes vivid. Tall conifer canopies are aerodynamically rough, and in humid regions they are often wet with intercepted rain. Evaporation from a wet canopy is not limited by stomata at all, so it responds directly to how fast the wind removes vapor.

Figure 2 shows this with the Penman–Monteith equation under identical weather. For a dry canopy, going from 1 to 5 m/s of wind raises transpiration by about 20%, over both grass and forest. For a wet forest canopy, the same change more than triples evaporation. Wind therefore matters most where the canopy is rough and wet, which matches where the authors observed the largest effects.

Figure 2. Increase in evaporation with wind speed, relative to 1 m/s, from the Penman–Monteith equation for a grass canopy and a 20 m conifer forest with the same canopy conductance (10 mm/s), and for the same forest when its canopy is wet with intercepted rain (no stomatal limit). Same weather in all cases: 150 W/m² of available energy, 20°C and a VPD of 1 kPa. Aerodynamic conductance from the logarithmic wind profile under neutral conditions. Figure by Daeha Kim, an illustrative calculation, not a result of Wang et al. (2026).

Leaves versus ecosystems

The result seems to contradict an earlier leaf-scale study, in which wind increased leaf WUE because it cooled sunlit leaves and so lowered their transpiration (Schymanski and Or 2016). The authors argue that the two are complementary. Leaf experiments last minutes under strong light, where convective cooling dominates. An ecosystem also loses water from soil and wet canopy surfaces, and over days these non-stomatal losses respond strongly to wind. What holds for a leaf does not automatically scale up to a forest.

Wind trends and the future

Near-surface winds over land weakened over several decades, a trend known as “stilling” (McVicar et al. 2012). For hydrologists, stilling is already familiar from the “pan evaporation paradox”: measured pan evaporation declined in many regions despite rising temperatures. Roderick and Farquhar (2002) traced the decline to dimming sunlight, and later work showed that weakening winds also contributed in many regions (McVicar et al. 2012). The new study adds a biological counterpart: weaker winds have let ecosystems fix carbon with less water.

The authors then used CMIP6 climate models, which reproduce the negative effect of wind on WUE, to estimate how wind trends will affect WUE in the future (Figure 3). In the historical period (1995–2014), declining winds raised WUE. By the end of the century, this wind-driven gain shrinks by about 80% under the low-emission SSP1-2.6, where stilling stops, and disappears under SSP2-4.5, where winds still weaken but WUE is less sensitive to them. Under the high-emission SSP5-8.5, stilling intensifies and the wind-driven gain in WUE stays about as large as in the historical period.

Figure 3. (a) Trends in near-surface wind speed over land in CMIP6 models for 1995–2014 and for 2081–2100 under three emission scenarios. (b) Trend in WUE caused by these wind changes, calculated as the sensitivity of WUE to wind multiplied by the wind trend. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Wang et al. (2026).

There is a feedback, too. Global greening makes the land surface rougher, which slows near-surface wind, which in turn raises WUE. Ecosystems are not only affected by wind; they help shape it.

Caveats

  • Daily relationships, not long-term experiments. The analysis uses day-to-day variation. Persistent changes in wind can also alter canopy structure, phenology and mortality, and those slower effects are not captured.
  • Wind trends are not smooth. Observations show that global terrestrial stilling reversed around 2010 (Zeng et al. 2019), which reminds us that wind trends can change direction within a decade.
  • ET partitioning remains uncertain. Separating transpiration from soil and canopy evaporation at flux towers is difficult, which limits how precisely the mechanism can be pinned down.
  • Models treat wind only indirectly. Earth system models represent wind through turbulence and the energy balance but have no explicit wind effects on stomata or photosynthesis.

What a hydrologist takes from it

WUE trends need wind in the attribution. If wind affects WUE as strongly as temperature or sunlight, part of the rise in WUE commonly attributed to CO₂ may reflect stilling. Studies that attribute long-term WUE trends should include wind speed as a driver.

Aerodynamic terms deserve the same attention as stomata. In much of ecohydrology, the canopy conductance gets the attention and the aerodynamic conductance is treated as a technicality. This study shows that at the ecosystem scale, the air side of the Penman–Monteith equation can dominate.

Interception is part of the carbon–water story. The strongest effects appeared where canopies are rough and often wet. Rainfall interception, a classic topic in forest hydrology, turns out to shape how efficiently ecosystems use water.

Bottom line

Across 146 flux towers, windier days lower ecosystem water use efficiency at four out of five sites, mainly because wind speeds up evaporation rather than because plants photosynthesize less. The effect is strongest in conifer forests and humid climates, where rough, often wet canopies lose water quickly to moving air. The long decline of winds over land has quietly raised WUE, and how much this continues depends on emissions. Wind belongs alongside CO₂, temperature and dryness as a driver of the carbon–water balance.

Questions to think about

  1. If part of the observed rise in WUE comes from stilling rather than CO₂, how would you design an analysis to separate the two?
  2. Why might the effect of wind on WUE be close to zero in arid climates, where VPD is high?
  3. Rainfall interception is often ignored in large-scale WUE studies. In a Korean forest catchment, how large would you expect the wet-canopy contribution to growing-season ET to be?

한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 물 이용 효율(WUE)은 생태계가 물 1 kg을 증발시키며 얻는 탄소의 양으로, 그동안 CO₂, 기온, 일사, 대기 건조도의 영향은 많이 연구되었지만 바람의 역할은 거의 다뤄지지 않았다. Wang 등(2026)은 전 세계 146개 에디 공분산 관측소 자료를 분석해, 다른 기상 요인의 영향을 제거해도 바람이 강한 날 WUE가 낮아지는 지점이 79.5%에 이르고 반대인 지점은 5.5%뿐임을 보였다. 풍속 1 m/s 증가당 WUE는 평균 약 0.26 gC/kg 감소했고, 상록침엽수림과 습윤 기후에서 가장 컸으며 건조 기후에서는 거의 0이었다. 원인은 주로 증발산 증가다. 바람은 기공을 더 열게 하는 것이 아니라 공기역학적 전도도를 높여 수증기를 더 빨리 실어 나르고, 대기를 더 건조하게 만든다. Penman–Monteith 식으로 계산해 보면 건조한 canopy의 증산은 풍속이 1에서 5 m/s로 늘 때 약 20% 늘지만, 차단된 빗물로 젖은 침엽수림 canopy의 증발은 세 배 이상 늘어 거칠고 젖은 canopy에서 바람의 영향이 가장 크다는 것을 알 수 있다. 지난 수십 년 동안 육상 풍속이 줄어든 현상(stilling)은 WUE를 조용히 높여 왔으며, CMIP6 전망에서는 이 효과가 저배출 시나리오에서 크게 줄고 고배출 시나리오에서는 현재 수준으로 유지된다. 따라서 장기 WUE 변화를 CO₂ 효과만으로 해석해서는 안 되며, 바람을 주요 요인으로 함께 고려해야 한다.

entry.title: How the brain invented learning, part I: steering in A Brief History of Intelligence

link.title: How the brain invented learning, part I: steering in A Brief History of Intelligence

entry.content:
The problems a worm solved 600 million years ago, and a fish solved 500 million years ago, look remarkably like the problems AI researchers ran into in the late twentieth century. Max Bennett’s A Brief History of Intelligence (2023) is built around that overlap.

Bennett is not a neuroscientist; he is an AI entrepreneur. That gives the book an unusual angle. He asks: at the points where we get stuck trying to build intelligence into machines, how, and in what order, did evolution get past them? His answer is organized into five “breakthroughs”: steering, reinforcing, simulating, mentalizing, and speaking.

This post covers the first, steering: the story of how bilaterian animals got the first brains. The second, reinforcing, the story of how early vertebrates acquired trial-and-error learning, follows in part II. The main characters in both are neurons, synapses, and dopamine, and each maps with surprising precision onto the weights of artificial neural networks and the reward signal of reinforcement learning.

The summary below is my own paraphrase of the book’s argument. A few connections, notably the three-factor learning rule, come from the broader neuroscience literature rather than from the book itself.

1. The birth of the neuron: speed was the price of eating

Neurons came before brains. And they evolved not for thinking, but because of how animals eat.

Plants and fungi live by absorbing sunlight or the nutrients around them. They have no reason to hurry. Animals took a different path: they eat other living things. Food moves, and you might be food yourself. That strategy demands a body that can respond quickly and as a whole. Chemicals diffusing slowly from cell to cell were not enough.

Neurons solve this. They carry electrical signals (action potentials) from one end of the body to the other almost instantly, then pass the signal to the next cell across a synapse using chemical messengers (neurotransmitters). The contrast is telling: sponges, which feed by filtering water, have no neurons, while cnidarians such as jellyfish have a diffuse nerve net spread across the body.

But a jellyfish’s nerve net mostly runs reflexes. A stimulus arrives, and a fixed response goes out. A central processor that pools many signals into a single decision, a brain, comes only in the next step.

The AI connection. The artificial neuron that McCulloch and Pitts proposed in 1943 is a radical simplification of the biological one: multiply the inputs by weights, sum them, and fire if the sum crosses a threshold. Synaptic strength became the weight, and whether a neuron fires became the activation function. Every layer of modern deep learning still rests on this abstraction.

2. Breakthrough 1, Steering: toward the good, away from the bad

The first brains appeared about 600 million years ago in bilaterians, animals with a head and a tail, a left and a right. Once a body has a front end, sense organs and neurons cluster there, and the animal becomes something that must decide which way to go.

The nematode C. elegans offers a living glimpse of what these early animals were like. With only 302 neurons, this tiny worm turns toward a strengthening food odor and away from a strengthening danger signal. It has no map and no representation of a goal. It moves on a single question: is this direction getting better or worse?

Bennett calls this the first breakthrough, steering. Its core is the ability to sort the world into good and bad, what neuroscientists call valence. Food odor is good; toxins are bad. This simple binary is where intelligence begins.

The original jobs of dopamine and serotonin

Remarkably, dopamine, the molecule we know as the “reward chemical,” is already present in this worm, but in a different role. In nematodes, dopamine roughly signals “something good is nearby.” When the worm is near food, dopamine is released, and the worm slows down to search the area thoroughly. Serotonin, by contrast, signals “I have eaten; I am full,” and makes the worm stop searching and rest.

At this stage, then, neuromodulators are less like messages carrying specific information and more like broadcasts that shift the state of the whole body. Bennett locates the origin of emotion here. Combinations of valence and arousal form primitive affective states, and these states make behavior persist. They are what keep the worm searching even when the food scent briefly fades.

The AI connection: Roomba

Bennett’s analogy is the Roomba robot vacuum. Rodney Brooks’s behavior-based robotics does not model the world in detail. Instead, it stacks simple reaction rules on top of sensor input to produce sensible-looking behavior. Bump into a wall, turn; find a dirty patch, scrub it longer. It is the same principle as the nematode’s steering.

The lesson is clear: useful, intelligent-looking behavior is possible without a model of the world. But a Roomba cannot learn from experience. The nematode went one step further, and the difference lies in the synapse.

3. Synaptic plasticity: the first learning

Bilaterians do more than run reflexes. Nematodes and the sea slug Aplysia both show associative learning. If food has always followed a particular odor, the odor alone becomes enough to draw them in. It is the same principle as Pavlov’s dog salivating at the sound of a bell.

The physical basis of this learning is synaptic plasticity: when two neurons are active together, the synapse between them strengthens. Donald Hebb proposed this rule in 1949, and it is often summarized as “neurons that fire together, wire together.” Eric Kandel used the simple circuits of Aplysia to show that learning is indeed stored as changes in synaptic strength, work that earned him the 2000 Nobel Prize.

Two problems that primitive learning already faced

Bennett makes a striking point here. Even the simplest associative learning already confronted two problems that AI still struggles with today.

First, the credit assignment problem. If several stimuli were present just before food was found, which one deserves the credit? Animals handle this with a handful of tricks:

  • Eligibility traces: only synapses that were active within a short window before the outcome are candidates for change.
  • Overshadowing: among several stimuli, the stronger or more salient one takes the association.
  • Latent inhibition: a stimulus that has often been experienced with no consequence is slow to acquire a new association.
  • Blocking: if one stimulus already predicts the outcome well, a newly added stimulus is not learned.

Second, the continual learning problem. How do you learn something new without losing what you already know? Artificial neural networks suffer from catastrophic forgetting: training on new data overwrites old knowledge. In animals, an extinguished association is not erased but suppressed. The evidence is spontaneous recovery, where the old response returns on its own after some time, and the fact that relearning is much faster than the original learning.

The AI connection: weights and the three-factor rule

Synaptic strength as a weight, and plasticity as a weight update, is a natural mapping. Stepping slightly beyond the book, there is a more precise one.

A pure Hebbian rule looks at only two factors: were the two neurons active together? In the real brain, a neuromodulator such as dopamine enters as a third factor. Co-activation leaves a trace at the synapse, and if dopamine is broadcast shortly afterward, that trace is consolidated into a lasting change. This structure, known in neuroscience as the three-factor learning rule, closely resembles how a single scalar in reinforcement learning (“that outcome was good”) modulates the direction of updates across the whole network.

In the nematode, dopamine still meant “something good is nearby.” The heart of the second breakthrough is that this signal became a more refined learning signal: “that was better than expected.”

4. The correspondence so far

The tables below pair each biological mechanism with its AI counterpart. The last column is my own judgment of how close the match is.

Groundwork

Biological mechanism AI counterpart How close
Neuron (action potential, fire or not) Artificial neuron (McCulloch–Pitts, activation function) Extreme simplification
Synaptic strength Weight Conceptually direct

Steering

Biological mechanism AI counterpart How close
Approach and avoidance by valence Reactive robots (Roomba, behavior-based robotics) Same principle
Global neuromodulator broadcast (dopamine, serotonin) Global scalar signal (reward, learning-rate modulation) Same principle
Synaptic plasticity (Hebbian rule) Weight update Different rules (local in the brain, backpropagation in deep learning)
Eligibility traces Eligibility traces (TD(λ)) Same term, same role
Spontaneous recovery after extinction Catastrophic forgetting Contrast: the brain suppresses, networks overwrite

5. Closing: a sense of good and bad, and a memory

Steering and synaptic plasticity gave the first brains two things: a way to sort the world into good and bad, and a way to store experience in the strength of synapses. Each maps neatly onto something in AI, from reactive robots to weight updates. But the nematode’s learning was about stimuli, not about its own actions, and its dopamine still meant only “something good is nearby.” How that signal became a learning signal, and why it turned out to match an algorithm AI researchers had already written down, is the subject of part II.

Questions to think about

  1. A Roomba behaves sensibly without learning anything. Which tasks in your own field could be handled by simple steering rules, and which need learning?
  2. Animals suppress old associations rather than erase them. What would an artificial network need in order to do the same?
  3. Eligibility traces, overshadowing, latent inhibition and blocking are the animal’s tricks for credit assignment. Which of them have counterparts in how scientists attribute an observed change to one of several possible causes?

한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). AI 기업가 Max Bennett는 『A Brief History of Intelligence』에서 지능의 진화를 다섯 번의 돌파 과정(steering, reinforcing, simulating, mentalizing, speaking)으로 정리하며, AI 연구자들이 막혔던 문제를 진화가 어떤 순서로 풀었는지를 다룬다. 이 글은 첫 단계인 조향(steering)을 다룬다. 약 6억 년 전 좌우대칭동물은 좋고 나쁨(valence)에 따라 다가가거나 피하기 시작했고, 함께 활동한 신경세포 사이의 연결이 강해지는 방식으로 경험에서 배우게 되었다. 그런데 이 단순한 학습도 오늘날 AI가 겪는 두 가지 어려움을 이미 안고 있었다. 하나는 먹이를 찾기 직전에 냄새, 빛, 온도 같은 여러 자극이 함께 있었다면 그중 어느 것을 기억해야 하는지 가려내는 일(신용 할당)이고, 다른 하나는 새로운 것을 배울 때 예전에 배운 것이 지워지지 않게 하는 일(지속 학습)이다.

Reference

Bennett, M. (2023). A Brief History of Intelligence: Evolution, AI, and the Five Breakthroughs That Made Our Brains. Mariner Books.
entry.summary: Notes on the first of Max Bennett's five breakthroughs: how the first neurons and brains appeared, how bilaterian worms learned to steer by good and bad, and how even their simple learning already faced problems that AI still struggles with.

entry.title: Why LLMs make things up, and what you can do about it

link.title: Why LLMs make things up, and what you can do about it

entry.content:
Anyone who uses large language models (LLMs) for research has met the problem: a confident answer, a plausible citation, and then the discovery that the paper does not exist. This is usually called hallucination. Here is what we know about why it happens, how much it has improved, and what users can do about it.

Hallucination, or confabulation

“Hallucination” is the popular term, but many researchers prefer confabulation, a word borrowed from neurology. A patient who confabulates fills gaps in memory with invented details and believes them, with no intent to deceive. That is close to what an LLM does: it produces fluent, specific and wrong content, with the same confidence as when it is right.

Farquhar et al. (2024) use confabulation for a narrower case: answers that are both wrong and arbitrary, so that asking the same question again gives a different answer. That distinction turns out to be useful, as we will see below.

Why it happens

A 2025 analysis by Kalai and colleagues at OpenAI gives the clearest explanation so far (Kalai et al. 2025). It has two parts.

Pretraining makes some errors unavoidable. A model learns by predicting text. For facts that appear many times in the training data, such as the boiling point of water, it learns the pattern. For facts that appear only once or rarely, such as a particular researcher’s birthday or the page numbers of a 2003 paper, there is no pattern to learn. The authors show that the error rate on such facts is tied to how many of them appear only once in training data. Bibliographic details, numbers, names and niche facts are exactly this kind of knowledge.

Training and evaluation reward guessing. Most benchmarks score an answer as right or wrong. “I don’t know” scores zero, the same as a wrong answer, so a model that always guesses scores higher than one that admits uncertainty. The authors compare it to a multiple-choice exam with no penalty for wrong answers: the rational strategy is to never leave a blank. Models were, in effect, trained to be good test-takers.

Why reasoning models do it less

Hallucination has dropped markedly over the past year, but not simply because models now “think” before answering. When OpenAI released its first strong reasoning model, o3, in 2025, it hallucinated more than its predecessor on an internal test of facts about people: 33% versus 16% for o1, because it made more claims overall (OpenAI 2025a). Reasoning gives a model more chances to be right and more chances to be wrong.

What changed is better explained by three things.

  1. Rewarding abstention. After the diagnosis above, labs began training models to decline when unsure. OpenAI reported that in its GPT-5 thinking model, the share of factual claims containing errors was 65% lower than in o3 (OpenAI 2025b).
  2. Using reasoning to check. Thinking time helps when a model uses it to test its own answer, not only to build a longer argument.
  3. Tools. Models that can search the web or read a supplied document answer from evidence instead of memory. Much of the improvement in everyday use comes from this.

The result shows clearly on AA-Omniscience, a benchmark by Artificial Analysis that asks hard factual questions without web access and, unusually, does not penalize “I don’t know” (Figure 1).

Figure 1. Out of 100 hard factual questions answered without web search, how many each model got right, got wrong, or declined (or answered only partly), for current models and two models released in November 2025. Wrong answers are computed as accuracy minus the AA-Omniscience Index. Gemini 4 Argon was not yet public when these results were recorded. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from AA-Omniscience results (Artificial Analysis) as compiled on 4 October 2026.

Which model hallucinates least?

As of October 2026, the answer depends on what you want.

  • Fewest wrong answers among frontier models: Gemini 4 Argon. It gets about half the questions right, declines most of the rest, and gives a wrong answer to only 8 in 100.
  • Best balance of knowing and admitting: Claude Opus 5.5 leads the AA-Omniscience Index (correct minus wrong), with GPT-6 Astra close behind. These models know more, so they answer more questions correctly, but they still guess on about 20 in 100.
  • Large differences remain: some capable models still answer almost every question and get about half of them wrong.

A year earlier, the leading models gave wrong answers to 33–40 questions in 100. The improvement is real. Two caveats apply. Rankings change every few months, and they differ between tasks: on summarizing a supplied document faithfully, a different leaderboard (Vectara’s) ranks models in another order. And no model is at zero.

What you can do

Even with the best model, the habits of the user matter more than the choice of model. These are the ones I find most effective, most of them also recommended by the model developers themselves (Anthropic 2026).

  1. Give it the source. Paste the paper, report or data, and ask it to answer only from that material. Asking for exact quotes first, and building the answer on them, works especially well for long documents.
  2. Give permission not to know. Say explicitly: “If you are not sure, say so.” This simple sentence counters the guessing habit described above.
  3. Turn on search for facts, and open the links. A cited source is only useful if it exists and says what the model claims. Check DOIs and page numbers yourself; this is where fabrication is most common.
  4. Ask twice. Ask the same factual question in a new conversation, or rephrase it. If the answers disagree, treat both as unverified. This is the practical version of Farquhar’s method, which detects confabulations from inconsistency across repeated answers.
  5. Ask for a separate check. After a draft, ask the model to list each factual claim and verify it, ideally in a fresh session. Splitting generation and verification reduces errors (Dhuliawala et al. 2023).
  6. Don’t lead the witness. “Isn’t it true that…?” invites agreement. Ask neutral questions, and be suspicious when the model simply confirms what you hoped.
  7. Know the danger zones. References, numbers, names, dates, recent events and very specialized facts are where models fail most. Reasoning, coding and explaining well-documented concepts are much safer.

Bottom line

Hallucination is not a mysterious bug. It follows from how models learn rare facts and from training that rewarded guessing. The newest models hallucinate much less, mainly because they have learned to say “I don’t know” and to check with tools, not just because they reason longer. The best defense is still on the user’s side: give the model the evidence, allow it to be uncertain, and verify anything that matters, especially citations and numbers.

Questions to think about

  1. Would you prefer a model that answers 66 of 100 questions correctly and 20 wrongly, or one that answers 50 correctly and 8 wrongly? Does your answer depend on the task?
  2. Kalai and colleagues argue that benchmarks should penalize wrong answers more than abstentions. How would that change how we grade students?
  3. Which of the seven habits above could you build into your group’s standard workflow for literature reviews?

한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). LLM이 그럴듯하지만 틀린 내용을 자신 있게 만들어내는 현상을 흔히 환각(hallucination)이라고 부르지만, 기억의 빈틈을 지어낸 내용으로 메우는 신경학 용어를 빌려 작화(confabulation)라고도 한다. Kalai 등(2025)에 따르면 원인은 두 가지다. 학습 데이터에 드물게 등장하는 사실(서지 정보, 수치, 인명 등)은 패턴으로 학습할 수 없고, 대부분의 평가가 “모른다”를 오답과 똑같이 0점 처리해 추측을 보상해 왔다. 추론 모델이라고 저절로 나아진 것은 아니어서, 2025년 o3는 이전 모델보다 오히려 더 많이 틀렸다. 최근의 큰 개선은 모를 때 답을 거절하도록 한 학습, 추론을 자기 검증에 쓰는 것, 검색 같은 도구 사용 덕분이다. 2026년 10월 기준 웹 검색 없이 어려운 사실 질문 100개를 풀게 하면, 틀린 답이 가장 적은 최상위 모델은 Gemini 4 Argon(약 8개)이고, 정답과 오답의 차이가 가장 큰 모델은 Claude Opus 5.5와 GPT-6 Astra(정답 63–66개, 오답 약 20개)이다. 1년 전 주요 모델은 오답이 33–40개였다. 사용자가 할 수 있는 일로는 원문 자료를 주고 그 안에서만 답하게 하기, “모르면 모른다고 하라”고 명시하기, 검색을 켜고 인용 링크와 DOI를 직접 확인하기, 같은 질문을 새 대화에서 다시 해 보기, 별도의 검증 단계를 두기, 유도 질문 피하기, 그리고 참고문헌·수치·인명·최신 정보처럼 오류가 잦은 영역을 특히 조심하기가 있다.

entry.title: Farm lime turns out to be a carbon sink

link.title: Farm lime turns out to be a carbon sink

entry.content:
Every year, American farmers spread tens of millions of tonnes of crushed limestone on their fields. The reason is simple: farming makes soils acidic, and acidic soils grow poorer crops. Climate accounting has long treated this practice as a small but certain source of carbon dioxide, since limestone is calcium carbonate and dissolving it can release CO₂.

A study published in Nature in September turns this assumption around (Suhrhoff et al. 2026). Using a century of records from the Mississippi River Basin, Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, Noah Planavsky and colleagues show that liming has, on balance, taken CO₂ out of the atmosphere. In an accompanying commentary, Philip Robertson and Stephen Hamilton, who reported early evidence of the same effect in Michigan almost twenty years ago (Hamilton et al. 2007), call it an unexpected carbon sink (Robertson and Hamilton 2026). The argument is a lesson in choosing the right baseline, and the decisive evidence comes from river water.

Why farmers lime

Soils become more acidic under intensive farming for several reasons. Nitrogen fertilizer and manure are converted by soil microbes into nitric acid. Burning fossil fuels has added sulfuric and nitric acid through acid rain. Decomposing soil organic matter adds more. In the cornfields of the US Midwest, natural processes cannot keep up, so farmers add lime (ground limestone or dolomite) to bring the soil pH back to where crops do best.

Two ways lime can dissolve

What happens to the carbon in lime depends on which acid dissolves it (Figure 1). When lime meets a strong acid such as nitric or sulfuric acid, its carbon is released as CO₂. When it meets carbonic acid, which forms when CO₂ from roots and microbes dissolves in soil water, the reaction goes the other way: it takes up CO₂ and stores it as bicarbonate. Bicarbonate drains into groundwater and rivers, reaches the ocean, and stays there for thousands of years. Soils are patchy, so both reactions happen side by side, and the balance between them decides whether lime is a net source or a net sink.

Figure 1. Lime that dissolves in strong acids releases CO₂; lime that dissolves in carbonic acid captures CO₂ as bicarbonate, which rivers carry to the sea. Strong acids release CO₂ even without lime, which is the baseline the new study uses. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic based on Suhrhoff et al. (2026) and Robertson and Hamilton (2026).

The missing baseline

The key step in the paper is a question about the counterfactual: what would happen if the acids were added but the lime were not? The strong acids do not disappear. They react with the bicarbonate already present in soils, groundwater and streams, and convert it to CO₂, which escapes to the air either on the spot or farther downstream. In other words, the CO₂ is released by the acid, not by the lime. Lime only determines where and how it happens.

Current inventories ignore this. The default method of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) assumes that all the carbon in applied lime ends up as CO₂, and the US national inventory assumes about half does. The authors argue that this kind of accounting gives the right answer only when lime inputs exactly balance acid inputs for a long time, which has rarely been true. The fair comparison is between “acid with lime” and “acid without lime”.

A century of acid and lime in the Mississippi Basin

The Mississippi River Basin is a natural test case. It covers 41% of the contiguous United States and about 65% of its cropland, and it receives most of the country’s agricultural lime. The authors reconstructed, county by county and year by year, how much acid and how much lime entered the basin since 1900.

Acid inputs roughly doubled to tripled over the century, from 450–800 moles per hectare per year in the early 1900s to 1,350–1,600 after 1970. Nitrification of fertilizer nitrogen now supplies about half of the total, a share that has grown as clean-air rules cut acid rain. Lime use rose sharply between 1935 and 1950, from about 1 million to about 20 million tonnes a year nationwide. Even so, lime has not kept pace with acid: by 2015 the basin had received about 20 trillion moles more acid than lime, roughly half of all the acid added. Lime is concentrated in the Corn Belt, where it offsets or exceeds the acid; much of the western basin receives acid but almost no lime.

What the model says

Feeding these inputs into a reactive transport model of soil chemistry, the authors compared CO₂ release with and without lime. In 1980, for example, the acids alone would have released about 20 million tonnes of CO₂ a year; with lime, the release fell to about 15 million tonnes (Figure 2a). The inventory methods, which count only lime, put the figure at about 7 million tonnes (IPCC) or 3.5 million tonnes (US inventory), and attribute all of it to the lime. Lime did cause a brief pulse of extra CO₂ when its use first surged in the late 1930s, because it first had to neutralize acidity already stored in the soil. After that, it lowered emissions.

What the river says

A model is only as good as its check against reality, and here the check comes from hydrology. The lower Mississippi has some of the longest water-chemistry records in the world, including alkalinity measurements kept by the New Orleans water utility and the US Geological Survey, which had already shown that the river’s bicarbonate export grew during the twentieth century (Raymond et al. 2008). When lime captures CO₂, the extra bicarbonate has to leave the basin through the river.

Comparing river bicarbonate fluxes with a pre-1935 baseline, the authors estimate that about 0.40 billion tonnes of CO₂ (±0.09) left the basin as lime-related bicarbonate between 1900 and 2015. If every bit of lime added since 1900 had reacted with carbonic acid, the maximum possible removal would have been 0.44 billion tonnes. About 90% of the potential has therefore been realized (Figure 2b). The soil model gives a lower but overlapping 0.22–0.37 billion tonnes, and changes in the river’s ratio of calcium and magnesium to bicarbonate point the same way. Losses of bicarbonate to deep groundwater, about 11% in this basin, are not counted and would add to the sink.

Figure 2. (a) CO₂ released by soil acid–base reactions in the Mississippi River Basin in 1980: modeled with anthropogenic acid inputs alone and with lime added, compared with the lime-only estimates of the IPCC default method and the US national inventory. (b) Cumulative CO₂ removed by lime, 1900–2015: the ideal maximum, the estimate from river bicarbonate records (with ±1 standard deviation) and the range of the soil model. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Suhrhoff et al. (2026).

The river also reveals a delay. Carbon removal shows up in the river decades after lime is applied. Calcium released by lime first sticks to soil particles and pushes off stored acidity, and the water then takes time to travel through soils and aquifers; groundwater in the Mississippi system is about ten years old on average. Tile drains, which carry water quickly from fields to ditches, probably shorten this delay.

What it means

For greenhouse-gas inventories, the source should be booked against the acid inputs, mainly nitrogen fertilizer and acid rain, rather than against the lime that neutralizes them. Counting lime as a source misrepresents the size, and over large areas and long periods even the sign, of its climate effect. It may also discourage farmers from keeping soil pH at the level that is best for crops.

For carbon markets, the picture is more nuanced. Robertson and Hamilton point out that liming at normal agronomic rates is ordinary practice, so it would not count as additional carbon removal deserving credit. The authors add a different warning: because ordinary liming is already a sink, projects that spread crushed rock to remove CO₂ (enhanced weathering) must not claim the removal that business-as-usual liming would have achieved anyway. In very acidic soils, lime may also release CO₂ first and remove it only years later, so short-term claims need care.

For agriculture, the result removes an apparent trade-off. Liming raises yields, improves soil health and can reduce emissions of other greenhouse gases; now it appears to remove CO₂ as well, at least at the scale of a large basin over decades.

The authors are careful about the limits. The estimate applies to the Mississippi Basin under its historical liming rates. Other regions, much heavier applications or very acidic soils may behave differently, and the modeled delay is uncertain by about 30 years across plausible hydrological settings.

What a hydrologist takes from it

Rivers are integrating sensors. A single sampling point near the mouth of the Mississippi summarizes the chemistry of 41% of a continent. Without that century-long record of alkalinity, this argument would rest on a model alone.

Long records are irreplaceable. The baseline before 1935 exists only because a city water utility kept measuring the river. Monitoring programs often look expensive and unexciting until a question like this one arrives.

Water travel times set carbon timescales. The delay between lime application and carbon export is partly a hydrological residence time. Questions about soil carbon removal are, in part, questions about how fast water moves through soils and aquifers.

Bottom line

Agricultural lime has been counted as a CO₂ source because dissolving limestone in acid releases CO₂. But the acid comes from fertilizer and pollution, and it would release CO₂ anyway by destroying bicarbonate in soils and rivers. Measured against that baseline, a century of liming in the Mississippi Basin has removed about 0.4 billion tonnes of CO₂, around 90% of its maximum potential, with a delay of decades. The finding calls for revising how inventories treat liming and shows how much a long river record can reveal about the carbon cycle.

Questions to think about

  1. If the CO₂ source is the acid rather than the lime, how would you change the carbon footprint of nitrogen fertilizer?
  2. Why might the decades-long delay between liming and river carbon export be shorter in tile-drained fields than in naturally drained ones?
  3. Many Korean upland soils are acidic and receive lime. Which river and soil data would be needed to test whether liming acts as a carbon sink in a Korean catchment?
